The driver has an unblemished record: 6.1 years on the platform, 1234 trips in 90 days, 0 disputes and 0 upheld deviations (F16), so no repeat-deviation escalation under RD-6 is warranted and the matter should be treated as a first notification-related incident under RD-7.
The dispute value is under $10 on the metered excess ($4.08, F4), so the system may rule finally under TH-1 and this route matter need not go to human review.

weaknesses: The call at 08:47 is a short 25 s call 'answered' but with no recording on record (F8), and RD-5 requires a call recording for verbal notice; the driver's written statement that she said 'ok' (F9) is a statement, not consent, and cannot be relied on.

There are no in-app chat messages at all (F7), so the entire notice case rests on the unrecorded call, and the rider's message quoted in the complaint says the line was bad — the other side will argue she never heard the reroute.

RD-3's road-name check points the other way for the driver's own account: F9 says he told her he would go via PRINCE CHARLES CRESCENT, which is among the roads driven in F3, but a statement made after the trip is not a rider consent message before the segment, and an agreed named road would still be checked against the segment record.

RD-4 traffic is matched only to the AYER RAJAH EXPRESSWAY band-2 reading at 08:41–09:06 (F10); the complained-of detour through TIONG BAHRU ROAD / ALEXANDRA ROAD is not itself on any jammed road, so the rider will argue the reroute was not a response to congestion on the replaced part of the route, and the weather was fair (F14).

points.response: Conceded as a statement of the records: the trip ran 13.5 km against 10.6 km optimal (+2.9 km, +27%) and the off-route segment added 2.58 km, so RD-1/RD-2 are engaged — but that establishes only that a refund is due, not that any goes to the driver.

True as far as it goes — the AYE sat at band 2 (10–19 km/h) from 08:41–09:06 (F10) — but a traffic reason is not a defence to the refund under RD-2; it decides only whether a driver violation is recorded, and the segment added 2.58 km (F3) at the rider's expense regardless.

A call log entry only proves a call occurred, not that notice was given or understood; RD-5 makes a call recording the evidence for verbal notice, and F8 records none, so the form of RD-5 is not satisfied.

The rider's complaint says the line was bad and no route was agreed, and there is no recording of what was said in the 25-second call (F8); a bad line cannot carry the specific reroute the driver claims, and it is not a rider message consenting to any route.

The driver's ceiling of $4.08 is exactly what we ask for: the excess distance fare of 2.89 km at $1.4101/km with surge at 1.0× (F4, F5), and we make no claim against the base, time or platform components (F6).

We do not seek a repeat-deviation flag (F16 shows 0 upheld route disputes), but RD-7 still applies independently of the driver's history: an uninformed reroute carries a notification-duty reminder, and $4.08 is still refunded.
Agreed that the $4.08 excess (F4) is under $10 and the system may rule finally under TH-1/TH-2, consistent with DISP-001.

Our own brief already conceded the call's form but not its content; the driver's own written statement (F9) admits he spoke of the route only after the fact of the choice, and D2's traffic point cannot convert an unrecorded call into rider consent.

Conceded as to the arithmetic: 13.5 km against 10.6 km optimal is +2.9 km (+27%) (F1) and the 08:59–09:06 segment added 2.58 km (F3), so the deviation exceeds the RD-1 tolerance and RD-2 is engaged. That only fixes the size of the pot; it does not decide whether the excess is refundable, which turns on RD-4 and RD-5.

RD-5 allows notice 'via in-app chat or phone', so the absence of in-app messages (F7) is not the same as absence of notice: the log shows the driver called the rider at 08:47, answered, 25 s (F8), which is a phone notice before the segment began at 08:59 (F3).

Conceded that the verbal notice is unproven as consent: the call (F8) has no recording on record and the driver's account (F9) is a statement made after the trip, which RD-5 says is not enough on its own. I therefore do not rely on F9 to exempt the segment.

I withdraw any named-road tie: the only source naming Prince Charles Crescent is the driver's own statement (F9), and no rider message exists before the segment began at 08:59 (F3, F7, F8), so on the record this segment is consent_after_or_none rather than an agreed named road.

Accepted that RD-4 does not shield the excess from refund, and I accept it: the AYE was at speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) from 08:41–09:06 (F10), a real congestion reason covering the segment (F3), so under RD-2's table a partial refund of the excess distance fare is the correct outcome and no driver violation should be recorded.

It follows from C5 that the quantum is not really in dispute: the excess distance fare is $4.08 (2.89 km × $1.4101/km, F4), surge is 1.0× (F5), and base, time and platform components of the $29.49 metered total (F6) are not refundable.
The rider's 3.7-year, 4.8-rating profile (F15) and the driver's 0 upheld route disputes in 90 days over 1234 trips in 6.1 years (F16) are agreed, and no flag_account applies under RD-6.

Under TH-1 the system may rule finally on a $4.08 refund, and DISP-001 shows an uninformed reroute being resolved automatically with the excess distance fare only; the notification-duty reminder and log under RD-7, with no formal warning for a first incident, is the appropriate rider-facing remedy alongside the refund.

notices.text: Your fare review is done, and you're getting money back. Your trip ran about 2.9 km longer than the most direct route, and the extra stretch was driven without proper notice to you, so that distance is being refunded. You'll get $4.08 back to the card or account you originally paid with; depending on your bank it can take a few days to appear. The rest of your fare stands. Nothing changes on your account, and you don't need to do anything.

We reviewed this trip. The route you drove was about 2.9 km longer than the most direct one, and the extra segment counts as an uninformed reroute — the call on record doesn't meet our notice rule, and a statement made after the trip doesn't count as rider consent. The $4.08 for that extra distance is being refunded to the rider's original payment method. There's no violation on your record and no formal warning; a traffic reason for that stretch is on file. This is a first occurrence, so we're sending a reminder about notifying riders when you take a longer route, and logging it. Please let riders know before or during the detour.
